title: Photography direction for a manufacturer
excerpt: Photograph the object and the step that makes it, at honest scale. Factory roofs, spark showers, and lobby portraits do not help a buyer judge the part.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights, for a piece on showing the product rather than the building.
caption: Goods on shelves, close enough to judge. A plant site should be this direct about the object. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the main photograph show?
faqs.answer: The object, with the feature that matters large enough to see, and a clue to scale. The real finish should survive retouching. A floating render with no reference makes every part look the same size and asks for trust before evidence.

faqs.question: Which factory photos should be rejected?
faqs.answer: Frames with no product. Roofs, lobbies, spark showers that hide the joint, and posed groups far from the work. They reassure an internal reviewer and teach a buyer nothing. One labeled shot of the cell or the inspection bench is more useful.

faqs.question: What should alt text say?
faqs.answer: What is in the frame. The object and the action, such as an inspector checking a housing in a fixture. Words like manufacturing or quality describe a mood, not a picture. Write the alt text while the shoot notes are still fresh.

markdown:
Manufacturer website photography has to show the object and how it is made. A buyer who needs specs and confidence is using the pictures as evidence. A factory cliché with no product, sparks and no part, a drone roof, a lobby, fails them. The frames are part of the argument. They are not a mood pasted under the headline.

Direct the shoot the way you would direct a sample. What must be visible, what scale is honest, what you refuse to fake. A founder can make these decisions before a photographer arrives. The decisions are about the offer, and the camera is there to record them.

## The object, large enough to judge

The primary frame is the thing you sell. Fill enough of the picture that a buyer can see the feature that matters. An edge, a finish, a joint, a label, a tolerance-critical face. If the feature is small, shoot it close and include one wider frame for context. A single heroic wide shot that makes every product look like a pebble will not survive a comparison with a competitor who showed the part.

Include scale. A hand, a fixture, a ruler, a known fastener. Manufactured objects lie about their size when they float on seamless paper with no reference. You can still light them carefully. The reference is the difference between a picture and a claim. If a dimension is the point of the product, consider a clean callout near the image on the page, and make the photograph agree with it.

Show the real finish. Retouching that removes the texture you actually deliver will create a painful first-article meeting. Dust, a stray fingerprint, and a messy bench can go. The grain, the weld, the weave, the anodize, the way a fabric breaks should stay. Ask the photographer to treat those as the subject. A buyer who needs confidence is looking for the surface they will receive, not for a render of a cousin of that surface.

If you make more than one family, do not let one beauty object stand for all of them unless you say so in the caption. A watch-like precision part and a structural weldment should not share a visual story that implies they are the same kind of work. Photograph the families you want inquiries for. Borrowed glamour from a product you no longer run is a form of drift.

## The process, in the frame

The second set of frames shows how the object is made, at the step that carries the argument. A fixture closed on the part. A person checking the critical characteristic. Material staged with its identity still readable, if that is something you are willing to show. Pack-out, if protection in transit is part of the offer. Choose steps a buyer can connect to their risk.

People belong in these frames when they are your people and they have agreed to be photographed. Hands at work are often more useful than faces lined up against a wall. A face is good on the about page when the role is named. On a process picture, the work is the subject. A posed group in clean coats, far from any object, slides back toward the cliché you are trying to avoid.

Shoot the sequence you would narrate in four beats. Incoming, the defining operation, the check, the pack. You will not use every frame on the homepage. You will use them across the homepage, the service, and a proof. Directing them as a set keeps the site from looking like five unrelated stock searches.

Reject frames that hide the product. The empty aisle at golden hour. The spark shower with the torch doing all the talking and the joint out of frame. The handshake over a miniature of the building. The hard-hat portrait against steel that could be any plant. They are easy to buy and easy to shoot, and they reassure the internal reviewer that the company looks like a manufacturer. The buyer learned nothing.

## A shot list a founder can hand over

Write the list before the day of the shoot. For each frame: the subject, what must be in view, what must be kept out, and the page it is for. "Homepage: housing on the fixture, sealing face visible, no clutter in the background, horizontal crop and a tighter vertical crop." That note prevents a beautiful set that does not fit the layout.

Include the boring frames. The spec sheet next to the part, if you want to show that documents exist. The label on the pack. The instrument at the bench. These will not win a photography prize. They will help a page whose job is confidence. Tell the photographer they are required, so they are not squeezed out by the more dramatic setups.

Plan for the phone. Ask for a composition that still shows the object when the sides are cropped away. A wide environmental frame with the part in the center-left will lose the part on a narrow screen, or it will shrink the part until it is a detail. Shoot a version where the object occupies the middle and survives a square crop. Art direction includes the crop the site will actually use.

Gather permissions in writing. Employees, customers' parts, logos that might appear on a fixture, neighboring tenants in a wide shot. A part that belongs to a customer is not yours to feature because it was on the bench that day. The proof page rules apply on set. When in doubt, turn the identifiable face of the customer's product away, or wait for approval.

## How the pictures sit in the layout

Place the object photograph where the first screen's argument needs evidence. The headline names the part. The picture shows it. The action, sales or a spec, stays visible. A full-bleed image that pushes the action below the fold on a laptop has won a design argument and lost the buyer's job. Scale the image so the evidence is there and the next step remains in view.

Captions should add the fact the picture cannot. The process step, the material, the role of the person. A caption that says "quality in everything we do" wastes the only line under the evidence. A caption that says "In-process check on the sealing face" tells the truth. Alternate text should describe the picture for someone who cannot see it, and it should match what is actually in the frame.

The [W3C's overview of WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) puts text alternatives under the first principle, perceivable. Non-text content needs a text alternative so people can reach the information another way. For these photographs, that means alt text that states the object and the action in the frame. "Team photo" or "manufacturing" fails. "Inspector checking a machined housing in a fixture" meets the requirement and helps anyone, including a buyer scanning on a slow connection who sees the text before the file.

Do not set type across the only view of the critical feature. Do not cover the part with a translucent brand panel. The picture is working. Treat it as a figure, with room to breathe, and let the words sit beside it or under it. Galleries that auto-advance should be used rarely. A buyer who was studying a finish will lose it when the carousel moves. If you show several frames, let the buyer advance them, and keep the first frame meaningful on its own.

## Files, weight, and color

These images are often the largest thing on the page, so they decide how fast the page starts. web.dev's [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) guidance uses Largest Contentful Paint for loading, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift for stability. A heavy hero that arrives late, or that shoves the headline when it loads, fails the first two impressions a buyer gets: what the part is, and whether the company is careful.

Export the sizes you will actually use. A phone crop and a wide crop, compressed, with dimensions reserved in the layout so nothing jumps. You do not need a lecture on formats to make the decision. Give the page real width and height, keep the file as small as the detail allows, and do not preload a background video of the factory in the same slot as the product.

Color should match the part. A grade that turns stainless into blue jewelry will mislead. Agree a reference on set, a physical sample under the light you care about, and look at the files on a normal laptop, not only on a calibrated retouching display. The buyer's screen is ordinary. The finish has to read there.

Keep a contact sheet and the selects in a place the team can find later. On a Hanabi project those files can live in the client portal with the brand documents, so the next page does not start from a scavenger hunt through a photographer's delivery link. The site and the library should point at the same chooses.

## Direction after the selects come back

Review selects against the shot list, not against a mood. For each required frame, mark pass or reshoot. A pass shows the object or the step, at honest scale, with permission. A near miss that is prettier than the pass is still a near miss if the feature is obscure. Be willing to reshoot a setup. The cost of a half day is smaller than a year of a homepage that hides the product.

Then edit the site's existing clichés out. If the new object photo is ready, remove the stock plant. Mixing one real frame with three generic ones makes the real frame look like an accident. Consistency is part of direction. The whole set should feel like it was made in the same place, because it was.

Write the alt text and captions while the shoot is still fresh, with the photographer's notes and the process owner's review. Waiting until launch week produces "image.png" and a caption that repeats the headline. The picture can carry a fact the headline does not, and someone has to write that fact down.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) when you want the photography and the page directed together. Bring the part, the step you are willing to show, and any limits from customers. The conversation should end with a shot list, not with a mood word.

Those frames will be judged first on a phone, where the crop is ruthless. [The mobile visit for a manufacturer](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-manufacturer) is the next piece, because the first screen on a small device still has to show the object, how it is made, and a way to reach sales or a spec.
